strengths: Addresses a timely and genuinely underexplored gap: most LLM UQ research targets single-turn or non-interactive multi-step settings, while agentic deployment increasingly demands UQ that accounts for information gained through interaction.

The graphical-model formulation (Definition 1, Figure 2) and the resulting factorization of trajectory probability provide a reasonably clean, general language that is shown to subsume single-step LLM UQ, multi-step reasoning UQ, and several aggregation schemes (max, weighted sum) used in prior work, which is a useful unifying exercise.

The core conceptual critique—that existing UQ methods treat uncertainty as monotonically, uni-directionally accumulating and thus cannot reflect uncertainty-reducing interactive actions (clarifications, tool queries)—is a clear and well-motivated diagnosis, illustrated concretely with the flight-booking example (Fig. 3).

The paper explicitly connects its formulation to established theoretical frameworks (PITMs, POMDPs, process reward modeling) and is transparent about the distinctions, which helps situate the contribution.

The discussion of practical implications across multiple domains (frontier LLM training, healthcare, coding, robotics) and the open-problems section are thoughtful and could stimulate follow-up work, even though they are speculative.
weaknesses: The paper provides zero empirical validation: no experiments, no case study with real numbers, not even a toy/synthetic demonstration that the proposed information-gating mechanism actually satisfies the stated desideratum (Eq. 1) or produces sensible uncertainty estimates. The authors explicitly state implementation is 'left for future work,' which makes the central practical claim of the paper (that this framework gives 'actionable guidance') unsubstantiated.

The proposed gating function g(·) is a fairly ad hoc hard switch between an MI-based reduction term and additive propagation, gated by a binary classification of actions into 'interactive & evidential' vs. not. No justification is given for why this specific functional form (rather than, e.g., a soft/continuous interpolation) is principled, and the 'evidentiality' notion presupposes solving a hard fact-verification subproblem that is left completely unaddressed.

The key quantity driving the reduction term, conditional mutual information between current observation and the initial query given trajectory history, is well known to be extremely difficult to estimate for open-ended natural language; the appendix acknowledges this but offers no concrete estimator, proof-of-concept, or error analysis, undermining the claimed 'actionability' of the framework.

Lemma 1 is a fairly mechanical corollary (plugging in the two extreme action-membership cases) rather than a substantive theoretical result, and it does not establish anything about tightness, achievability, or usefulness of the bounds for real trajectories.

There is substantial conceptual overlap with an already-published position paper on the same topic (Kirchhof et al., 2025b, cited in this manuscript, ICML Position Paper Track: 'UQ needs reassessment for LLM agents'), and this submission does not clearly delineate what novel technical insight it adds beyond additional formalism and an unimplemented gating proposal.

Several central design choices (e.g., treating the environment transition as deterministic, assuming reliable observations, using a fixed binary action taxonomy in Table 1/2) are acknowledged as simplifying but are not stress-tested, so it is unclear how robust the framework is once these assumptions are relaxed, which the authors themselves flag in Limitations.

As primarily a conceptual/notational contribution without empirical grounding, the paper does not meet the reproducibility and adequacy-of-evidence bar typically expected even for Findings-level acceptance, since there is no way to verify that the proposed reformulation yields better calibrated or more useful uncertainty signals than existing methods.

strengths: Identifies a timely and genuinely important gap: most LLM UQ research still treats generation as a static, single-turn or non-interactive multi-step process, while real agents operate under open-world, multi-turn interaction where uncertainty can be resolved rather than merely accumulate.

The graphical-model formulation (Def. 1/2, Fig. 2) is a reasonably clean unifying abstraction that shows how single-step LLM UQ, multi-step reasoning UQ, and several aggregation strategies (max, weighted sum, tail confidence) are special cases of a general trajectory-level decomposition via the entropy chain rule.

The 'conditional uncertainty reduction' perspective and the information-gating idea (distinguishing interactive/evidential vs. non-interactive actions) is a conceptually appealing and intuitive contribution that could inspire concrete follow-up methods.

Related work coverage is thorough and the practical-implications section usefully surveys plausible application areas (healthcare, coding agents, robotics), which may be valuable for orienting future researchers even if speculative.
weaknesses: The paper contains zero empirical validation: no experiments, no benchmark results, no implementation of the proposed gating mechanism, action classifier, or uncertainty estimators. Every core mechanism (interactivity/evidentiality classifier, mutual-information estimation, initial-query and observation uncertainty estimation) is explicitly deferred to 'future work,' so the central claim that this framework yields more reliable, reward-predictive uncertainty estimates (Eq. 1, the 'desideratum') is never tested, not even on a toy example.

Much of the 'general formulation' (Sec. 3) is a fairly mechanical application of the entropy chain rule to a graphical model; while it is a useful organizing device, it does not constitute new theoretical insight, and the subsequent 'unified view' largely just re-labels known aggregation heuristics (mean, max, weighted sum) as special cases without new analysis of their properties.

Lemma 1's 'extrema' bounds are trivial corollaries of the chain-rule decomposition combined with the assumption that all/no actions fall in the reduction set 𝒜−; they provide little practical guidance since realistic trajectories mix action types, and no bound or approximation is offered for the mixed, realistic case.

The information-gating function g(·) that operationalizes 'reducible uncertainty' hinges on a binary, hand-specified action taxonomy (interactive+evidential vs. not) that is illustrated only qualitatively in tables (Table 1, Table 2) sourced from example trajectories, with no validation that such classification is learnable, reliable, or that the resulting signed uncertainty actually correlates with task success.

The desideratum in Eq. 1 (calibrated uncertainty should be predictive of reward) is stated as the target criterion for the whole framework but is never connected back analytically or empirically to the proposed gated uncertainty measure — there is no proof or demonstration that the conditional-reduction formulation actually satisfies it better than the accumulation baseline it criticizes.

Section 5 (practical implications across healthcare, coding, robotics) and Section 6 (open problems) are largely speculative essay-style discussion with citation-supported assertions rather than argued or evidenced claims tied to the paper's formal contribution; they read as scope-expanding padding rather than substantiating the core claims.

The paper's own stated assumptions (reliable observations, deterministic environment transitions) are precisely the conditions least likely to hold in the 'open world' interactive settings the paper argues are essential, undermining the applicability of the very formalism proposed, and this tension is acknowledged only in the Limitations section without any mitigation.

As a purely conceptual/vision paper with no reproducible artifact (no code, no data, no worked numerical example even on the running toy scenario), it does not meet the reproducibility bar generally expected for a soundness-based recommendation, despite the manuscript's framing of itself as providing 'actionable guidance.'

strengths: Identifies a genuinely important gap: most LLM UQ work assumes a static, non-interactive system, while real agentic deployments involve multi-turn interaction that can resolve (not just accumulate) uncertainty. This is a timely and well-motivated observation.

Provides a clean, rigorous formalization (Definition 1/2, the dynamic Bayesian network in Fig. 2) that is shown to subsume several existing UQ setups (single-step QA, multi-step reasoning, weighted aggregation schemes) as special cases, giving the framework good explanatory/unifying power.

The information-gating mechanism and the derived analytic upper/lower bounds (Lemma 1) offer an interpretable, principled way to think about when uncertainty should increase vs. decrease, tied to action interactivity and evidentiality.

Extensive, well-organized discussion of practical implications across multiple domains (healthcare, coding, robotics, frontier LLM training) and a thoughtful open-problems section that could stimulate follow-up empirical work.

Clear writing, good use of illustrative running examples (flight-booking / τ-bench), and an honest limitations section acknowledging the simplifying assumptions (reliable observations, deterministic environment updates).
weaknesses: The paper is purely conceptual: there is no experiment, empirical validation, or even a toy simulation showing that the proposed conditional uncertainty reduction framework actually satisfies the stated desideratum (Eq. 1) or outperforms/differs meaningfully from prior accumulation-based UQ in practice. All central claims about the practical benefit of the framework remain untested.

The core operational components (action classifier for interactivity/evidentiality, estimators for action/observation uncertainty, mutual information estimation between observation and initial query) are only sketched at a high level (Sec. 4.2, Appendix D) and explicitly deferred to 'future work,' leaving the feasibility and reproducibility of the proposed method largely unverified.

The gating function and its 'valid uncertainty reduction action set' 𝒜⁻ are defined somewhat ad hoc (a binary interactive+evidential criterion) without justification of why this particular gating rule is the right one versus alternative parameterizations; no sensitivity analysis or ablation is possible without an implementation.

Several strong claims (e.g., 'first general formulation of agent UQ,' desiderata framed as hard inequalities) are asserted without empirical or even simulated support, which is a weaker standard of evidence than typically expected for such definitive claims.

As a position/framework paper without any implementation, dataset, or code, reproducibility in the ACL Rolling Review sense (independent verification of a concrete result) is essentially not applicable, which is a concern for a research contribution at this venue.
